title: Is SaaS taxable in Alabama? What software sellers should check
summary: Review Alabama software tax rules before treating SaaS as exempt. Learn what the state guidance establishes and how SSUT differs from a taxability decision.
body_markdown:
Do not assume every product labeled SaaS is exempt in Alabama. The Department of Revenue says software transactions are taxable, while separately stated services that accompany a software transfer can receive different treatment.


That guidance does not, by itself, resolve every hosted-access contract. The source reviewed here does not establish a blanket exemption for all SaaS. If your conclusion depends on customers receiving only a hosted service rather than taxable software rights, document the facts and obtain advice specific to that sale.


## What the official guidance says


Alabama's[software tax guidance](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/ador-issues-guidance-on-taxability-of-computer-software/) discusses the distinction between conveying software and providing related services. The marketing label and billing frequency do not establish which transaction you made.


Question Evidence to review


Does the customer receive software or a right to use it? License and contract terms


Is the product hosted only, downloaded, or delivered with hardware? Product design and delivery records


Are services separately stated? Contract and invoice


Does the product mix software and other work? Scope and pricing for each component


Avoid using “custom” as an automatic exemption either. The state's guidance does not limit taxable software transactions to off-the-shelf products.


## What is Alabama SSUT?


The[Simplified Sellers Use Tax program](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/sales-use/simplified-sellers-use-tax-ssut/) lets eligible, approved remote sellers collect a flat 8% tax on covered taxable sales.


SSUT is a collection method. It does not turn a nontaxable service into a taxable sale, and it does not mean every Alabama business may use the flat rate.


Review eligibility and your Alabama presence before applying. Do not switch an existing tax setup to 8% merely because it is easier to configure.


## Economic nexus and marketplace sales


For remote sellers, Alabama's collection threshold is **more than $250,000 in direct Alabama retail sales in the prior calendar year** . The calculation includes taxable and nontaxable retail sales. It excludes qualifying wholesale sales and sales through a participating SSUT marketplace that collects Alabama tax for the seller. Physical presence can create duties below that threshold. See the Department's[remote seller FAQ](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/faqs/are-all-remote-sellers-required-to-register-in-alabama/) .


Keep direct and marketplace sales separate. A marketplace's tax collection does not cover purchases made through your own website.


## How to register and file


1. Check product taxability, Alabama presence, and the remote seller threshold.
2. If eligible for SSUT, apply through[My Alabama Taxes](https://myalabamataxes.alabama.gov/) using “Obtain a new tax account.” Wait for approval before collecting SSUT.
3. Apply the approved rate to taxable sales and keep the tax separate on the invoice.
4. File and pay SSUT each month by the **20th of the following month** . Follow the[program's electronic payment cutoff](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/sales-use/simplified-sellers-use-tax-ssut/) .


Outside SSUT, Alabama's[general state rate is 4%](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/sales-use/state-sales-use-tax-rates/) , and local taxes may apply. Use the[current local rate files](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/sales-use/local-cities-and-counties-tax-rates-text-file/) rather than a statewide combined-rate estimate. Standard sales tax returns are generally due monthly on the 20th; the Department can approve a less frequent schedule for eligible sellers under its[filing rules](https://www.revenue.alabama.gov/sales-use/sales-tax/) .


For example, an approved SSUT seller with a taxable $100 sale collects $8. That example assumes the sale is taxable and the seller belongs in SSUT; neither follows merely from the customer being in Alabama.


## How to make a defensible SaaS decision


Prepare a short description of what the customer buys, where the software runs, whether any copy transfers, and what services accompany it. Attach a sample contract and invoice.


Have the tax reviewer connect those facts to Alabama authority. If the treatment remains unclear, seek a determination through the Department of Revenue's published channels rather than treating a third-party state matrix as conclusive.


## What to keep in billing records


Keep the approved classification, effective date, customer location, and any exemption evidence. Separate tax from revenue and reconcile credits to the original transaction.


Review the decision when you add downloads, hardware, or a new service. See[sales tax software for AI and API companies](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/sales-tax-software-ai-api-companies) for ways to test the resulting setup.


For sales in other states, use the[SaaS sales tax guide](https://www.afternoon.co/blog/SaaS-sales-tax-guide) to find the relevant state rules and plan the registration review.
